title: Muscles: Origin, Insertion, Action, and Innervation
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter teaches the muscles that board questions return to most often: the rotator cuff, the muscle groups served by the major limb nerves, the cranial nerve muscles of the head and neck, and the trunk muscles of posture, breathing, and the pelvic floor. The emphasis is on reasoning rather than memorizing lists. If you know where a muscle pulls, which compartment it lives in, and which nerve serves that compartment, you can work backward from a weakness, a deformity, or an abnormal gait to the injured nerve and the level of injury. Most exam items give exactly that kind of clue.
prerequisites: Bones and bony landmarks of the scapula, humerus, pelvis, femur, tibia, and fibula
Brachial and lumbosacral plexus organization: roots, trunks or divisions, cords, and terminal branches
Joint movements and planes: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, inversion, eversion
Upper versus lower motor neuron signs

connections.to: Neuroscience: peripheral nerves and spinal cord
connections.how: Root, plexus, and peripheral nerve lesions each leave a distinct pattern of weakness, sensory loss, and reflex change.

connections.to: Embryology of the pharyngeal arches and somites
connections.how: A muscle keeps the nerve of the arch or somite it came from, which explains V3 to the chewing muscles, VII to the face, and XII to the tongue.
The diaphragm generates most of the quiet tidal volume, so phrenic nerve and high cervical cord injuries present as ventilatory failure.
Rotator cuff tendinopathy and tears are degenerative tendon disorders shaped by the anatomy of the subacromial space.
The levator ani supports the pelvic organs and maintains the anorectal angle, linking pelvic floor injury to prolapse and incontinence.

terms.def: The usually proximal, more fixed attachment of a muscle.
The usually distal, more mobile attachment that the muscle pulls toward its origin.
A group of muscles enclosed by fascia that share a function and, as a rule, a single motor nerve.
Two muscles pulling in different directions on a bone so that their combined effect is rotation rather than translation.
The supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis, whose tendons blend with the shoulder joint capsule and hold the humeral head in the glenoid.
The gap between the humeral head and the coracoacromial arch, through which the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa pass.
Hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints with flexion of the interphalangeal joints, caused by loss of the lumbricals and interossei.
Drop of the pelvis on the unsupported side during single-leg stance, caused by weakness of the hip abductors on the stance side.
Inability to dorsiflex the ankle, so the toes catch the ground during the swing phase of gait.
The posterior branch of a spinal nerve, supplying the deep (intrinsic) back muscles and the skin over them.
The levator ani and coccygeus, which together form the muscular floor of the pelvic cavity.

blocks.text: The glenohumeral joint trades stability for range: a large humeral head sits on a shallow glenoid fossa, deepened only slightly by the glenoid labrum. The loose capsule cannot hold the head in place through the full arc of motion, so stability depends on four muscles whose tendons fuse with the capsule on its superior, posterior, and anterior sides. Together they form the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis). Each muscle produces its own movement, but their shared job is to press the humeral head into the glenoid while larger muscles move the arm. The capsule is not reinforced by the cuff inferiorly, which is why most dislocations are anterior and inferior.

blocks.title: Rotator cuff muscles
rows: Middle part of lateral border of scapula
blocks.caption: Three muscles reach the greater tubercle from behind; only subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle from the front.

blocks.text: Abduction shows why the cuff matters. With the arm at the side, the deltoid (axillary nerve) pulls almost straight upward along the humerus, so on its own it would slide the head up into the acromion rather than swing the arm out. The supraspinatus pulls the head medially into the glenoid, and the infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis pull it downward. This force couple converts the deltoid's pull into rotation. Classic teaching gives the supraspinatus the first 15 degrees and the deltoid the range to about 90 degrees; throughout the movement the trapezius and serratus anterior rotate the scapula upward, and that rotation is what allows the arm to rise above about 90 degrees.

blocks.title: Why the supraspinatus is the cuff tendon that fails
steps: Tendon runs under the coracoacromial arch
Abduction and overhead use narrow the subacromial space
Tendon is compressed against the acromion repeatedly
Age-related degeneration weakens the tendon near its insertion
Tendinopathy, then partial or full-thickness tear
Painful arc; weak initiation of abduction
blocks.caption: Impingement plus degeneration explains why supraspinatus tears are most common and rise with age.

blocks.text: Injury patterns follow the nerves. The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament, then around the spinoglenoid notch; entrapment at the first site weakens both abduction initiation and lateral rotation, while entrapment at the second weakens lateral rotation alone and wastes only the infraspinatus. The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so a surgical neck fracture or anterior dislocation weakens the deltoid and teres minor and numbs the skin over the lower deltoid, sparing the supraspinatus. Infraspinatus remains a strong lateral rotator in that case, so lateral rotation is only mildly weak. Subscapularis loss is tested by the patient's inability to push the hand away from the lower back (lift-off test).

blocks.predict: A patient cannot start abducting the arm from the side, but if the examiner lifts the arm to 30 degrees, the patient can continue to raise it. Which muscle is likely torn?
blocks.explain: The supraspinatus. Once the arm is partly abducted, the deltoid has a better line of pull and can continue the movement even without the supraspinatus.
blocks.check: The abduction paragraph and the force couple.

blocks.text: Each upper limb compartment has a principal nerve: anterior arm (musculocutaneous), posterior arm and forearm (radial), most of the anterior forearm and thenar eminence (median), and most intrinsic hand muscles (ulnar). The lesion site along the nerve decides which branches are lost.

blocks.title: Upper limb nerves, muscles, and deficits
rows: Weak elbow flexion and supination; lost biceps reflex
Dorsum of hand over first web space
Most forearm flexors, thenar muscles, lateral two lumbricals
Wrist: ape hand. Elbow: also hand of benediction
Palmar lateral three and a half digits
Flexor carpi ulnaris, medial profundus, hypothenar, interossei, medial lumbricals, adductor pollicis
Elbow or wrist: claw of digits 4 and 5, weak finger abduction
Medial one and a half digits
blocks.caption: Root values vary slightly between texts.

blocks.text: Elbow flexion is weakened rather than abolished because the brachioradialis (radial nerve) still flexes the elbow, and supination survives through the supinator (radial nerve). The radial nerve spirals in the radial groove of the humerus, so a midshaft fracture paralyzes the wrist and finger extensors and the wrist hangs flexed (wrist drop); the triceps is usually spared because its branches leave above the groove. Compression in the axilla, as from a crutch, also weakens the triceps.

The median nerve enters the hand through the carpal tunnel and sends its recurrent branch to the thenar muscles. Compression there (carpal tunnel syndrome) or a wrist laceration weakens or paralyzes opposition and thumb abduction, the thenar eminence wastes, and the thumb lies in line with the fingers (ape hand). In carpal tunnel syndrome palm sensation is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum. A lesion at the elbow, as in a supracondylar fracture, also paralyzes the flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of the profundus, so on attempting a fist the index and middle fingers stay extended (hand of benediction).

blocks.title: How ulnar nerve loss produces a claw hand
steps: Medial lumbricals and interossei are paralyzed
MCP flexion and IP extension of digits 4 and 5 are lost
Extensor digitorum hyperextends the MCP joints unopposed
Long flexors flex the IP joints
Claw of the ring and little fingers
blocks.caption: Digits 2 and 3 are spared because the median nerve supplies their lumbricals.

blocks.text: The ulnar nerve also supplies all the interossei, so a card cannot be gripped between the fingers, and loss of adductor pollicis makes the patient flex the thumb tip with flexor pollicis longus (median nerve) to pinch paper (Froment sign). Clawing is paradoxically worse with a lesion at the wrist than at the elbow, because a distal lesion spares the medial flexor digitorum profundus, which then flexes the distal joints strongly. The long thoracic nerve lies on the surface of the serratus anterior in the medial axillary wall, exposed during axillary node dissection. The serratus holds the scapula against the chest wall and rotates it upward, so its loss lifts the medial border away when the patient pushes against a wall and limits abduction above the horizontal.

blocks.title: Localizing an ulnar nerve lesion
blocks.text: A cyclist has clawing of digits 4 and 5, weak finger abduction, and a positive Froment sign, with numbness of the palmar little finger but normal sensation over the dorsal medial hand and strong ulnar wrist flexion. The dorsal cutaneous branch and the branch to flexor carpi ulnaris leave the nerve in the forearm, so sparing both places the lesion at the wrist (Guyon canal). The marked claw fits, because the medial flexor digitorum profundus is intact. An elbow lesion would add weak ulnar wrist flexion and dorsal hand numbness, with a milder claw.

Lower limb deficits are also read by compartment. The femoral nerve (L2 to L4, posterior divisions of the lumbar plexus) supplies the anterior thigh; the obturator nerve (L2 to L4, anterior divisions) supplies the medial thigh; the sciatic nerve divides into the tibial nerve for most of the posterior thigh, the posterior leg, and the sole, and the common fibular nerve for the anterior and lateral leg. The superior gluteal nerve (L4 to S1) supplies the hip abductors.

blocks.title: Lower limb nerves, muscles, and deficits
rows: Weak knee extension, lost patellar reflex, numb anterior thigh and medial leg
Pelvic surgery, retroperitoneal hematoma, femoral catheterization
Adductor longus, brevis, and magnus (adductor part), gracilis
Weak adduction; leg swings outward; numb medial thigh
Pelvic surgery, pelvic tumor, difficult labor
Gluteus medius and minimus, tensor fasciae latae
Foot drop, steppage gait, weak eversion, numb dorsum of foot
Fibular neck fracture, tight cast, leg crossing
Gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior, long toe flexors, sole muscles
Weak plantarflexion and inversion, cannot rise on toes, lost ankle reflex, numb sole
Popliteal fossa trauma; tarsal tunnel (distal branches)
blocks.caption: The nerve's compartment predicts the movement lost; its course predicts the cause.

blocks.text: Femoral injury makes the knee buckle on stairs or uneven ground, because the quadriceps can no longer lock it; the saphenous branch carries sensation from the medial leg. Hip flexion is only mildly affected because the psoas major receives direct branches from the lumbar plexus.

During walking, each limb in turn bears the body weight alone, and that weight falls medial to the stance hip. The gluteus medius and minimus of the stance limb pull on the pelvis to keep it level. When they are paralyzed by a superior gluteal nerve injury, the pelvis tilts down on the side of the lifted leg. The pelvis therefore drops on the side opposite the lesion, while the lesion is on the stance side.

blocks.title: Trendelenburg sign from a right superior gluteal nerve injury
steps: Patient stands on the right leg; left foot lifts
Body weight acts medial to the right hip
Right gluteus medius and minimus cannot hold the pelvis
Pelvis drops on the left (unsupported) side
Trunk lurches right to shift weight over the hip
blocks.caption: Positive sign: pelvis drops opposite the weak abductors. The lurch is the compensation.

blocks.text: The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin, which makes it the most often injured nerve of the lower limb. Its deep branch supplies the dorsiflexors and its superficial branch the evertors, so the foot hangs plantarflexed and inverted, the toes drag, and the patient lifts the knee high to clear them (steppage gait). Inversion is preserved because tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve lies deep in the popliteal fossa and is injured much less often.

blocks.title: Foot drop: common fibular nerve or L5 root?
blocks.text: Both lesions cause foot drop and numbness over the dorsum of the foot, because the L5 root supplies the dorsiflexors through the common fibular nerve. The difference lies in muscles that receive L5 through other nerves. Tibialis posterior (tibial nerve, L4 and L5) inverts the foot, and the gluteus medius (superior gluteal nerve, L4 to S1) abducts the hip. In an L5 radiculopathy both are weak, so inversion and hip abduction are reduced, and back pain often radiates down the leg. In a fibular neck lesion inversion and hip abduction are normal, and the history usually involves the fibular neck itself (fracture, cast, prolonged leg crossing). Testing inversion is the key step.

sections.title: Head and neck muscles and their cranial nerves

blocks.text: Head and neck innervation follows embryologic origin. Muscles that develop from a pharyngeal arch keep that arch's nerve: first arch muscles are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), and second arch muscles by the facial nerve (CN VII). The tongue muscles come instead from occipital somites and migrate forward carrying the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).

blocks.title: Muscles of mastication (first arch, CN V3)
rows: Lateral ramus and angle of mandible
Sphenoid wing and lateral pterygoid plate
Neck of mandible, TMJ disc and capsule
blocks.caption: Three muscles close the jaw; the lateral pterygoid opens it, aided by the suprahyoids and gravity.

blocks.text: Because each lateral pterygoid pulls its own condyle forward, a CN V3 lesion makes the chin deviate toward the paralyzed side on opening, as the intact muscle advances only the healthy condyle. The masseter and temporalis waste on that side, and the jaw jerk is lost. CN V3 also supplies the other first arch muscles (mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini).

The muscles of facial expression insert into skin. Key members are the frontalis (raises the eyebrows), orbicularis oculi (closes the eye), orbicularis oris (closes the lips), buccinator (keeps the cheek against the teeth so food stays between them), and platysma. CN VII also supplies the stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric. A lower motor neuron lesion such as Bell palsy paralyzes the whole half of the face, including the forehead; the eye cannot close, food collects in the cheek, and loss of stapedius makes sounds seem too loud. An upper motor neuron lesion, such as a cortical stroke, spares the forehead because the part of the facial nucleus serving the upper face receives corticobulbar fibers from both hemispheres.

The tongue has intrinsic muscles that change its shape and extrinsic muscles that move it: genioglossus (protrudes), hyoglossus (depresses), styloglossus (retracts and elevates), and palatoglossus (elevates the back of the tongue). All are supplied by CN XII except palatoglossus, which develops with the palate muscles and is supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X) through the pharyngeal plexus.

blocks.title: Why the tongue deviates toward a CN XII lesion
steps: Each genioglossus pulls the tongue forward and toward the opposite side
Both sides acting together protrude it in the midline
One genioglossus is paralyzed
Intact genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side
Lower motor neuron lesion: weak side atrophies and fasciculates
blocks.caption: The protruded tongue points toward the lesion.

blocks.text: The sternocleidomastoid runs from the manubrium and medial clavicle to the mastoid process. Acting alone it turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head toward its own shoulder; together they flex the neck. The trapezius elevates, retracts, and depresses the scapula and, with the serratus anterior, rotates it upward for overhead reach. CN XI arises from the upper cervical cord, enters the skull through the foramen magnum, and leaves through the jugular foramen. Injury in the posterior triangle, often at lymph node biopsy, spares the sternocleidomastoid (already supplied) but paralyzes the trapezius, so the shoulder droops and the arm cannot be raised fully overhead.

blocks.predict: A patient cannot shrug the right shoulder and has difficulty turning the head to the left. Where along CN XI is the lesion likely to be?
blocks.explain: Proximal, at or near the jugular foramen. The right sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the left, so its weakness plus trapezius weakness means the nerve was injured before it supplied the sternocleidomastoid. A posterior triangle lesion would spare head turning.
blocks.check: The sternocleidomastoid and CN XI paragraph.

sections.title: Trunk muscles: back, diaphragm, abdominal wall, and pelvic floor

blocks.text: Trunk muscles fall into two developmental groups. Epaxial muscles form behind the vertebral column and are supplied by dorsal rami; hypaxial muscles form the body wall in front and are supplied by ventral rami. The erector spinae is the main epaxial group. Its three columns (iliocostalis laterally, longissimus, spinalis medially) arise by a common tendon from the posterior iliac crest, sacrum, and lumbar spinous processes and insert on the ribs, vertebrae, and skull. Acting together they extend the spine; acting on one side they bend it laterally. Superficial back muscles such as the trapezius and latissimus dorsi are limb muscles that migrated onto the back and are not supplied by dorsal rami.

blocks.title: Trunk muscles at a glance
rows: Extends and laterally flexes the spine
External oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis
Compress abdomen; flex and rotate trunk
Thoracoabdominal (T7 to T11) and subcostal (T12); L1 branches to the lowest internal oblique and transversus
Supports pelvic viscera; maintains anorectal angle
Nerve to levator ani (S4) and pudendal branches
blocks.caption: Dorsal rami supply the deep back; ventral rami supply the rest.

blocks.text: The diaphragm arises from the xiphoid process, the lower six costal cartilages, and the lumbar vertebrae (through the crura and arcuate ligaments), and inserts into its own central tendon. When it contracts, the dome descends and the lower ribs are raised, enlarging the thorax, lowering intrapleural pressure, and drawing air in. In quiet breathing it generates most of the tidal volume. Its motor supply is the phrenic nerve from C3 to C5, mainly C4, because its muscle precursors arise at cervical levels and descend with their nerve. The phrenic nerve is also sensory to the central diaphragm, so irritation there refers pain to the shoulder (C3 and C4 dermatomes).

blocks.title: Cervical cord level and breathing
steps: Complete injury at or above C3: phrenic output lost, apnea
Injury at C4 to C5: diaphragm partly spared, ventilation impaired
Injury below C5: diaphragm works, intercostals and abdominals lost
Below C5: weak cough and forced expiration
blocks.caption: Unilateral phrenic palsy instead gives an elevated hemidiaphragm that moves paradoxically upward on a sniff.

blocks.text: The anterolateral abdominal wall has three flat layers with crossing fiber directions (external oblique running inferomedially, internal oblique superomedially, transversus abdominis horizontally) and the vertical rectus abdominis in its sheath. Contracting together, they raise intra-abdominal pressure for forced expiration, coughing, defecation, and childbirth. Their nerves are the continuations of the lower intercostal nerves (thoracoabdominal, T7 to T11) and the subcostal nerve (T12), with the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) to the lowest fibers. These run between the internal oblique and transversus, so supply and skin sensation are segmental, with T10 at the umbilicus.

The levator ani is a thin muscular sheet stretching from the pubis, the tendinous arch over the obturator internus fascia, and the ischial spine to the perineal body, anococcygeal body, and coccyx. Its tone supports the bladder, uterus, and rectum, and it contracts reflexly whenever intra-abdominal pressure rises. The puborectalis slings the anorectal junction forward, holding the anorectal angle that contributes to fecal continence; it relaxes during defecation. Stretching or tearing of the levator ani and its nerves during vaginal delivery is a major cause of pelvic organ prolapse and stress urinary incontinence.

blocks.predict: During a hard cough, why does urine leak in a woman with a weakened pelvic floor but not in one with a healthy pelvic floor?
blocks.explain: The abdominal wall and diaphragm raise intra-abdominal pressure. Normally the levator ani contracts at the same moment, supporting the bladder neck and urethra so urethral closure pressure rises with bladder pressure. Without that support, bladder pressure exceeds urethral pressure and urine leaks.
blocks.check: The levator ani paragraph and the abdominal wall actions.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology together explain innervation. Arch muscles keep the arch nerve (V3, VII, and the vagus for the palate and pharynx), somite-derived tongue muscles keep CN XII, epaxial back muscles keep dorsal rami, and the diaphragm keeps the cervical phrenic nerve after descending. In the limbs, compartments developed as dorsal and ventral muscle masses supplied by posterior and anterior divisions of the plexuses, which is why one nerve serves one functional group and why a single deficit localizes so well. Neuroscience adds the next layer: a peripheral nerve lesion affects one nerve's muscles and skin, a root lesion affects every muscle sharing that segment across several nerves, and an upper motor neuron lesion weakens movements with spasticity and brisk reflexes rather than wasting.

Pathology supplies the mechanisms of injury: compression at fixed tunnels (carpal tunnel, suprascapular notch, fibular neck), traction or laceration during fractures and surgery, degeneration of poorly vascularized tendons, and stretching of the pelvic floor in childbirth. Physiology explains the consequences, from the lost force couple in a rotator cuff tear to hypoventilation after phrenic injury. Real anatomy varies, so the classic patterns described here are the starting point for reasoning, and electrodiagnostic testing or imaging confirms the site in practice.

summary: The rotator cuff holds the humeral head in the shallow glenoid; supraspinatus initiates abduction, infraspinatus and teres minor rotate laterally, and subscapularis rotates medially.
Suprascapular nerve: supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Axillary nerve: teres minor and deltoid. Supraspinatus is torn most often because it is compressed under the coracoacromial arch.
Upper limb: musculocutaneous loss weakens elbow flexion, radial loss causes wrist drop, median loss at the wrist causes ape hand, and ulnar loss causes clawing of digits 4 and 5.
Claw hand results from paralyzed lumbricals and interossei, which leaves MCP joints hyperextended and IP joints flexed.
Long thoracic nerve injury paralyzes serratus anterior and wings the scapula; it is a classic complication of axillary surgery.
Lower limb: femoral loss weakens knee extension, obturator loss weakens adduction, common fibular loss causes foot drop with weak eversion, and tibial loss weakens plantarflexion and inversion.
In a Trendelenburg sign the pelvis drops on the lifted side; the weak gluteus medius and minimus are on the stance side.
CN V3 supplies mastication, CN VII facial expression, CN XII the tongue except palatoglossus (CN X), and CN XI the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
Diaphragm: phrenic nerve C3 to C5; complete cord injury at or above C3 causes apnea. Abdominal wall: T7 to T12 and L1 in a segmental pattern.
Erector spinae extends the spine on dorsal rami; levator ani supports the pelvic organs, and puborectalis holds the anorectal angle.

verify: The supraspinatus is taught as initiating abduction over about the first 15 degrees; electromyographic studies show it active throughout abduction with the deltoid. Confirm the classic framing NABNE expects.
Root values for peripheral nerves (for example subscapular C5 and C6, sometimes C7; median C6 to T1, sometimes C5 to T1; superior gluteal L4 to S1) vary slightly between texts.
Innervation of the levator ani is described differently across sources (nerve to levator ani from S3 to S4 or S4, with variable pudendal contribution); confirm the version NABNE uses.
The share of quiet tidal volume produced by the diaphragm is quoted from about two thirds to about 75 percent; the chapter states only that it produces most of it.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects eponyms and named tests (Froment sign, hand of benediction, Guyon canal, lift-off test, Bell palsy) or only the descriptive findings.

The term hand of benediction is used for the median nerve lesion at the elbow (on attempting a fist) in most anatomy texts, but some review books apply it to the ulnar claw; confirm the usage NABNE expects.
